newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-LVMH clears big hurdle in DFS bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-LVMH clears big hurdle in DFS bid.

text.p: French luxury goods flagship LVMH cleared a big hurdle in its bid for control of the American duty free chain DFS after a U.S. arbitrator approved the contested $2.47 billion deal.

LVMH said on Wednesday the arbitrator gave a green light to DFS shareholders seeking to sell 58.75 percent of the San Francisco-based chain to LVMH despite the opposition of minority shareholders seeking to block the takeover.
"The world's leading luxury goods group thus acquires the world's leading retailer of luxury goods," LVMH said in a statement.
It said the deal would boost its operating profit by around 30 percent and increase its sales -- which totalled 29.8 billion francs in 1995 -- by close to 50 percent.
Shares in LVMH rallied seven percent on the Paris bourse as investors applauded the deal, which reinforces LVMH's presence in the lucrative Pacific Rim market.
It would also strengthen LVMH's control over the distribution of its luxury products, ranging from Moet & Chandon champagnes to Christian Dior perfumes and Louis Vuitton luggage.
"The fact that the arbitrator has given approval removes uncertainty hanging over the deal," a Paris trader said.
But the acquisition still requires clearance from U.S. regulatory authorities examining the antitrust implications.
The dissident DFS shareholders also signalled on Wednesday that they would not leave quietly and that they intended to ensure that LVMH abided by the terms of the arbitration accord.

The accord drawn up by arbitrator Ira Millstein, recruited to resolve the DFS shareholders' dispute under the terms of the original partnership, stipulates among other things that LVMH must sign an agreement guaranteeing DFS's long-term autonomy.

One of the dissident shareholders, Robert Miller, said in a statement that the agreement "imposed stringent conditions on LVMH's ability to achieve synergies at the expense of DFS and its suppliers who compete directly with LVMH products".

He said he and another dissenting shareholder Tony Pilaro "will closely monitor LVMH's adherence to restrictions on integrating DFS into its operations. There are serious antitrust issues, and DFS suppliers have told us they are cooperating with the FTC as it reviews LVMH's recent Hart-Scott-Rodino filing".
LVMH filed with the FTC last week, and French newspapers report that it requested an expedition of the process, which normally takes a month.

LVMH, which has a long tradition of allowing its many brands to retain their identities, said in its statement that it was committed to preserving the autonomy of DFS and had invited DFS chief executive officer Myron Ullman to remain in his job.
It said DFS has an "exceptional" track record, with an operating margin averaging 15 percent over the past three years and 85 percent return on equity.
LVMH shares were up 7.5 percent at 1,336 francs at 1230 GMT.
